title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Understanding a software company begins not with its marketing acronyms, but with who signs the purchase order, how the code touches their daily workflow, and when cash actually clears the bank.
epigraph.author: Institutional Field Notes

web_blocks.html: SoftTech Engineers operates across the AECO (Architecture, Engineering, Construction, and Operations) software chain [3][4]. It serves both public urban agencies and private real estate builders [3][4]. Recently, management grouped legacy brands—AutoDCR, PWIMS, Opticon, and RuleBuddy—into the cloud-native CIVIT Suite [4]. That suite spans three lifecycle pillars: Plan, Build, and Sustain [4].

SoftTech's revenue model blends three distinct streams, unlike pure enterprise SaaS firms [2][3][4]. First are one-time project setup, custom work, and license fees for government bodies [2][3][4]. Second are recurring SaaS, pay-per-use scrutiny fees, and Annual Maintenance Contracts (AMCs) [2][3][4]. Third are third-party hardware pass-throughs and IT services [2][3][4]. Per the H1 FY27 Investor Presentation, recurring sales jumped 46.2% YoY to ₹28.21 Cr [3]. That lifted recurring mix from 37.5% of standalone sales in FY26 to 43.5% in H1 FY27 (and 45.7% in Q2 FY27) [3].

rows: AutoDCR & RuleBuddy: Automated CAD/BIM building-plan scrutiny and municipal permit workflow
PWIMS: Public works project lifecycle, tendering, billing, and infra monitoring (e.g., AAI, JNPA)
Opticon: Construction ERP for private contractors/developers (BOQ, procurement, costing)
Transferable Development Rights (TDR) digital registry & trading platform
Customization, GIS/BIM services, third-party hardware/stock-in-trade pass-through
web_blocks.takeaway: Civit PLAN/PERMIT (AutoDCR) remains the core profit and growth engine at 52.1% of H1 FY27 mix. Meanwhile, Civit INFRA is inherently lumpy and Civit BUILD remains sub-3% despite years of investment.

web_blocks.html: A key nuance in the audited FY26 P&L is Purchase of Stock-in-Trade [2]. In FY26, SoftTech spent ₹20.87 Cr on stock-in-trade (net of ₹1.66 Cr inventory change = ₹19.21 Cr COGS) [2]. That equals 14.5% of consolidated sales, up from ₹16.82 Cr net in FY25 [2]. The spend covers bundled third-party licenses, cloud/GIS tools, and hardware for large turnkey projects [2][3]. Examples include the ₹92.95 Cr Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority Integrated Command & Control Centre order [3]. Thus, SoftTech is not an 85%-margin pure SaaS firm. Gross margin after stock-in-trade is ~85.5%, yet heavy staff and project costs bring EBITDA margin to ~24.2% [1][2].

web_blocks.title: Concrete End-to-End Example: How AutoDCR / CivitPERMIT Works in Mumbai & Pune
paragraphs: Picture an architect filing a 20-storey residential tower plan in Pune (PMC) or Greater Mumbai (MCGM) [16][17]. Under the old manual system, the architect submitted physical paper blueprints [16][17]. Municipal engineers then checked setbacks, stair widths, fire-tender access, and Floor Space Index (FSI) by hand [16][17]. Reading hundreds of pages of Development Control Rules took months and invited subjective disputes [16][17].

With AutoDCR (now CivitPERMIT), the architect drafts the plan in CAD/BIM using set layer rules and uploads it online [16][20]. SoftTech's geometry engine parses every polygon and checks room sizes, parking ratios, and FSI against local rules [16][20]. It flags rule errors on the drawing within minutes and routes clean files to issue demand notes and final permits [16][20]. SoftTech earns an upfront setup fee from the city plus a pay-per-use fee per square foot or application [3][4].

web_blocks.html: Beyond municipal permits, SoftTech has expanded into two newer verticals. First is CivitINFRA for large central and state agencies [3][9]. Key wins include the Airports Authority of India (AAI) and the ₹92.95 Cr JNPA AI Digital Twin project [3][9]. Second is CivitTDR / eTDR, a digital registry for Transferable Development Rights in metro cities [3]. It scaled from 0% to 3.2% of standalone sales in H1 FY27 (and 5.3% in Q2 FY27) [3]. Meanwhile, private construction ERP (CivitBUILD, formerly Opticon) and global BIM bids (CivitTWIN, Finland, Middle East) remain small [3]. CivitBUILD was just 2.8% of H1 FY27 mix, and consolidated PAT fell 4.9% YoY after an MEA order delay [3].

A close look at the subsidiary footprint shows how concentrated the core engine remains [2][3]. The group lists nine domestic and global subsidiaries across Finland, Germany, Dubai, the UK, Singapore, the US, and India [2]. Yet standalone parent sales of ₹128.30 Cr generated 96.5% of FY26 consolidated revenue (₹132.90 Cr) [2]. The other subsidiaries added just ₹4.60 Cr of sales while cutting consolidated PBT by ₹4.06 Cr [2]. Inside India, however, CivitPERMIT's rollouts across Maharashtra, Delhi (DDA), Jammu & Kashmir, and 18 states offer a strong base for eTDR and digital twins [3][16][17]. Converting that domestic municipal base into steady pay-per-use cash remains management's core operational test [3].

web_blocks.mechanism: Built deep regulatory workflow software (permitting, courts, property tax) embedded inside local governments, then transitioned from upfront licenses to recurring SaaS and transaction-based citizen fees.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Recurring revenue climbed past 75% of total sales with operating margins above 20% and high customer retention (>98%) because switching municipal systems of record carries severe operational risk.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Municipal permitting software can become a sticky annuity if pay-per-use adoption scales, but only if implementation customization does not permanently trap engineering headcount and working capital.

book_paragraphs: If you ask ten investors what SoftTech Engineers does, nine will say 'building-plan approval software' and stop there. That is half true, and the other half is where the financial complexity lives. Yes, SoftTech's heart and soul is AutoDCR, now rebranded as CivitPERMIT, which accounts for just over half of standalone revenue in H1 FY27.

Let's walk through what happens on the ground so you can picture the product clearly. Imagine you are an architect in Mumbai or Pune designing an apartment block. Before you can pour concrete, the municipal corporation must verify that your building obeys hundreds of local Development Control Rules: setbacks from the road, fire-escape widths, parking bays, and allowable Floor Space Index. Years ago, you carried physical rolls of blueprints to a ward office, where an engineer pulled out a scale ruler and checked them by hand. Every ambiguity was an invitation for delay.

SoftTech encoded those municipal rules into a CAD geometry engine. Today, the architect uploads a digital CAD or BIM drawing to the municipal portal, and SoftTech's software reads the polygons, checks every rule automatically, highlights any non-compliant wall or corridor on the drawing itself, calculates the scrutiny fee, and routes the file digitally for sign-off. Over 1,500 cities across 18 Indian states have used this engine.

Now here is the part you and I need to watch closely: SoftTech is trying to turn that municipal foothold into a four-pillar AECO platform, adding CivitINFRA for ports and airports, CivitBUILD for private contractors, CivitTDR for development-rights trading, and digital twins for global markets. Some of those extensions, like eTDR and JNPA's digital twin, are gaining traction; others, like private-sector CivitBUILD, remain under 3% of sales after years of effort.

Let's also check where the revenue actually comes from geographically. If you look at the standalone Indian parent in FY26, it generated ₹128.30 Cr of revenue and ₹12.99 Cr of profit before tax. The entire consolidated group generated ₹132.90 Cr of revenue and ₹8.93 Cr of profit before tax.

Do that quick subtraction with me: all of SoftTech's international and domestic subsidiaries combined added just ₹4.60 Cr of net revenue while subtracting ₹4.06 Cr from pre-tax profit! That tells you immediately that 96.5% of SoftTech's real commercial engine is still right here in India, powered by AutoDCR, PWIMS, and domestic urban local bodies.

That is also why the new domestic modules matter so much. Civit eTDR, which digitizes Transferable Development Rights trading in metro cities, went from zero in H1 FY26 to 5.3% of standalone sales in Q2 FY27. And the ₹92.95 Cr JNPA port digital twin contract shows SoftTech can sell higher-ticket infrastructure command-and-control platforms to Indian public-sector undertakings.

Let us walk inside each of SoftTech's operating segments so you can picture how a rupee of revenue is actually earned on the ground. At the core sits CivitPERMIT, formerly AutoDCR, which automates building-plan scrutiny for municipal corporations, state town-planning departments, and special development authorities. Imagine an architect in Mumbai or Pune submitting a 40-story residential tower plan: instead of waiting six months for a municipal engineer to manually verify floor-space index (FSI), setback margins, fire-tender access, and parking ratios, the architect uploads a standardized CAD/BIM drawing into CivitPERMIT. Within minutes, the rule engine flags every violation against local Development Control Regulations.

Around that core, management has layered CivitINFRA (public works and infrastructure project management, including PWIMS), CivitBUILD (construction ERP and contractor billing via Opticon), and CivitPLAN / eTDR (transferable development rights and urban planning). Most recently, the ₹92.95 Cr JNPA contract showcases SoftTech's push into port-scale AI Digital Twins and integrated command centers, combining geospatial mapping, IoT telemetry, and asset lifecycle workflows into a single enterprise deployment.

Notice the crucial economic difference between these segments. Pure pay-per-use CivitPERMIT scrutiny fees, where architects or citizens pay a small transaction fee per building permit, carry software-like gross margins and fast cash collection. By contrast, large turnkey e-governance and digital-twin contracts with ports, airports, or state bodies require heavy customization, third-party hardware or GIS integration, milestone-based billing, and months of waiting for government sign-offs. When you see H1 FY27 standalone recurring revenue grow 46.2% YoY to ₹28.21 Cr while consolidated unbilled contract assets sit at ₹53.52 Cr, you are watching those two business models pull the company in opposite directions.

book_callouts.title: Pure SaaS vs. Hybrid Turnkey Reality
book_callouts.text: Notice that SoftTech spent ₹19.21 Cr net on 'purchase of stock-in-trade' in FY26—roughly 14.5% of revenue. When a software company wins port command-centre or turnkey government projects, third-party hardware and licenses dilute gross margins and tie up working capital.

book_subsections.title: Why Recurring Mix Matters—And Where the Mix Still Stings
paragraphs: Management rightly highlights that recurring revenue, SaaS subscriptions, pay-per-use scrutiny fees, and AMCs, grew 46.2% YoY in H1 FY27 to ₹28.21 Cr, reaching 43.5% of standalone sales. When an architect pays a per-application or per-square-foot fee to run a plan check, SoftTech collects cash upfront without waiting eighteen months for a municipal treasury department to clear an invoice.

Yet 56.5% of standalone revenue is still one-time project, implementation, and services work. In CivitINFRA, which dropped from 29.0% of H1 FY26 mix to 11.2% in H1 FY27 before the big ₹92.95 Cr JNPA order, revenue arrives in lumpy milestones. And in Services & Others (30.8% of H1 FY27 mix), margins are structurally lower than pure software IP.

Until recurring pay-per-use and SaaS revenue crosses 65–70% of consolidated sales, SoftTech will remain a hybrid GovTech systems integrator and product company, subject to government budget cycles and lumpy milestone billing.

callouts.title: Watch the Subsidiary Drag
callouts.text: In H1 FY27, standalone PAT jumped 69.5% YoY, yet consolidated PAT fell 4.9% YoY due to an MEA order deferment and overseas subsidiary costs. Always underwrite the consolidated P&L, never the standalone headline.

book_subsections.title: Inside a Typical CivitINFRA & eTDR Deployment
paragraphs: To make CivitINFRA concrete, consider how a major port or airport authority manages capital works. Previously, contractors submitted paper measurement books, Excel progress trackers, and disjointed CAD drawings. When SoftTech deploys CivitINFRA, as at the Airports Authority of India or Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority, it builds a centralized digital twin and command dashboard that links geospatial GIS maps, 3D BIM models, contractor billing milestones, and physical site progress.

Similarly, in cities like Mumbai or Pune, Transferable Development Rights (TDR) are tradable certificates worth crores of rupees that allow developers to build extra floor area. Historically, TDR verification was paper-heavy and prone to title disputes. Civit eTDR creates a digital ledger and bidding/verification workflow where every TDR certificate is linked to municipal GIS and AutoDCR approvals, allowing SoftTech to clip a small transaction fee on high-value urban real-estate activity.

callouts.title: Follow the Cash, Not the Acronym
callouts.text: Whether SoftTech calls a product AutoDCR or CivitPERMIT, PWIMS or CivitINFRA, the economic test is identical: does it collect recurring pay-per-use fees upfront, or does it sit as unbilled milestone work on the balance sheet?

book_subsections.title: The Contrast Between Recurring SaaS and Turnkey Digital Twins
paragraphs: Picture two very different customer invoices sitting inside SoftTech's accounting system. Invoice A comes from a mid-sized architectural firm in Maharashtra paying a pay-per-use CivitPERMIT scrutiny fee on a 12-unit apartment block: the software runs automatically on cloud servers, the fee is collected digitally upfront, and gross margin is north of 85%. Invoice B comes from a multi-year state infrastructure or port authority contract like the ₹92.95 Cr JNPA AI Digital Twin deployment: it involves custom GIS modeling, on-site integration, multi-department user acceptance testing, and milestone billing.

In H1 FY27, standalone recurring revenue climbed 46.2% YoY to ₹28.21 Cr (43.5% of standalone sales). This is the strongest operational bright spot in the entire SoftTech story. The risk is that the remaining 56.5%. And the consolidated subsidiaries, remain tethered to lumpy turnkey milestones where cash collection lags revenue recognition by six to twelve months.
